To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there were earlier SOS (start-of-season), later EOS (ending-of-season), longer LOS (the length of the growing season) and greater MaxNDVIS from north to south, while there was a significantly delayed EOS (the ending-of-season) in the southern Yamal Peninsula, which might be attributed to anthropogenic impacts.
there were earlier SOS, later EOS, and longer LOS from north to south along the latitudinally varying gradients in western Arctic Russia.

(i) there is a north–south phenological gradient of SOS and LOS, but not of EOS and MaxNDVI, along latitudinal gradients in western Arctic Russia, (ii) the phenological changes in recent decades were not consistent in western Arctic Russia and the phenological changes were mainly caused by temperature, and (iii) anthropogenic factors could play an important role in the phenological change in the southern part of western Arctic Russia.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the detection of the impacts of climate changes and anthropogenic factors on vegetation phenology in the Yamal Peninsula, which is the first step in understanding the response of high-latitude ecosystems to environmental changes.
a comprehensive understanding of the phenological shifts in the western Arctic region and the associated factors.

a better understanding of the phenological shifts in the Yamal Peninsula in response to climate change and human activities, as well as the uncertainties in remotely-sensed phenological detection in northern high latitude ecosystems.

the vegetation in the Yamal region is responding to climate changes, but the responses are complicated by anthropogenic impacts, which are difficult to separate.
climate change is the dominant driver of phenological change in the western Arctic region.
the observed phenological trends in the western Arctic Russia were mainly driven by climate change and anthropogenic activities.

the phenological changes in the western Arctic are complex and should be monitored using multiple satellite data.

the spatial patterns of phenological parameters in northern high latitudinal ecosystems are highly heterogeneous and are controlled by multiple factors including temperature and anthropogenic activities.
there is a significant delayed EOS in western Arctic Russia based on AVHHR data, but not based on MODIS or VGT data.

the AVHRR data should be used cautiously for monitoring phenological changes in northern high latitudinal regions.
there is a significant delay in the end of the growing season in the western Arctic region of Russia, but this is not a general phenomenon in the Arctic region.
there is a strong need for more accurate and consistent monitoring of vegetation phenology in high latitudes.
